description: We’re a group of six students who share a love for game design, programming, and astrophysics. We’re more than excited to create an interactive space mission game where players can engage with the adventure of designing, managing, and simulating a complete space mission.
summary:
Mission Forge is a browser game where the player runs a space mission from start to finish. You pick a ship, then you fly it through a real mission. You collect science and try to reach orbit. Every choice has a cost. Speed or shields. Afterburner or staying power. Which ship you pick changes how the mission plays out. The goal is to let anyone feel the pressure of a space Mission in a few minutes, not in an entire semester. 
Choose your ship. Three options, each with real trade-offs.
Aegis V-1 Interceptor: fast (38 km/s, 75 km/s afterburner), but only 100 HP shields.
Odyssey IX Explorer: balanced (32 km/s, 65 km/s afterburner, 120 HP).
Titan Heavy Cruiser: slow (26 km/s, 52 km/s afterburner), but 160 HP shields.
Fly the mission. Navigate through gates. Dodge asteroid belts. Keep the ship alive.
Collect science data orbs. Every orb you grab adds to your mission outcome.
Reach orbital capture. This is the finish line. How much science you bring back depends on the choices you make along the way.
details:
What does it do, or how does it work?

Mission Forge is a browser game where you run a space mission from start to finish. You pick one of three ships. Each ship has different speed, afterburner, and shield stats. Then you fly the mission. You navigate through gates, dodge asteroid belts, and collect science data orbs along the way. Your goal is to reach orbital capture and bring back as much science as you can.

There is no best ship. The Aegis V-1 is fast but fragile. The Titan is slow but tough. The Odyssey sits in the middle. How you fly and what you pick changes how the mission goes. You make the trade-off, then you live with it.

What benefits does it have?

A student can learn what mission trade-offs feel like in about five minutes. No install, no account, no setup. You send someone the link, and they are playing in ten seconds.

The benefit is that the hard part of mission design stops being a paragraph in a textbook. Instead of reading about mass limits and power budgets, you feel the cost of a choice. You pick the fast ship and find out it cannot take a hit. You pick the tough ship and find out it is too slow to grab every orb. That is the lesson, and you learn it by doing, not by reading.

What is the intended impact?

We want students who have never touched a space mission to walk away understanding one thing: every mission is a set of trade-offs, and you cannot have everything.

That is the same problem real mission designers face. They do not get the fast ship and the tough ship at the same time. They pick what matters and accept what it costs.

If a student plays Mission Forge for five minutes and then asks, "Wait, what if I picked the other ship?", we did our job. That question is the whole point.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • React and TypeScript for the game itself
  • A 3D renderer running in the browser for the space visuals
  • Hosted on Netlify so anyone can play from a link
  • Built and tested on regular laptops, no special hardware

We kept the stack simple on purpose. The game has to run on a school laptop and a projector at the same time.

How is your project creative?

Most space games hand you one ship and ask you to fly it well. We did the opposite. We made the choice to ship the first real decision, and we balanced the three ships so none of them is the safe pick.

The fast ship is not better. The tough ship is not better. Each one asks you to fly differently. That is what makes it feel like a mission design problem instead of an arcade shooter.

We also kept the goal simple: reach orbit, collect science. The complexity is in the choice, not in the controls. Anyone can pick it up.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Balance. If one ship were clearly the best, the game would be broken. We tested each ship to make sure the trade-off actually mattered.
  • Time. We had one hackathon. We cut what we could not finish and kept what worked. The flight and the ship choice are done. A fuller mission designer and a debrief screen are the next step.
  • Who is playing? We assumed the player had never played a space game. That meant clear ship stats on the first screen, a simple goal, and controls you can learn while playing.
  • Where it runs. It has to work in a browser, on a normal laptop, with no setup. That ruled out anything heavy or anything that needs an install.
